The Quantization Trap: Breaking Linear Scaling Laws in Multi-Hop Reasoning

Henry Han ††thanks: Corresponding author: henry_han@baylor.edu Affiliation: School of Engineering and Computer Science, Baylor University, Waco, TX 76798, USA    Xiyang Liu Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China, 710126    Xiaodong Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author: wangxiaodong1021@gmail.com Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China, 710126    Fei Han Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Communication Engineering, Jiangsu University, Zhenjiang, 212013, China    Xiaodong Li Affiliation: Beijing Electronic Science and Technology Institute, Beijing 100070, China
Abstract

Neural scaling laws provide a predictable recipe for AI advancement: reducing numerical precision should linearly improve computational efficiency and energy profile (E∝bitsE\propto\text{bits}). In this paper, we demonstrate that this scaling law breaks in the context of multi-hop reasoning. We reveal a ’quantization trap’ where reducing precision from 16-bit to 8/4-bit paradoxically increases more net energy consumption while degrading reasoning accuracy. We provide a rigorous theoretical decomposition that attributes this failure to hardware casting overhead, the hidden latency cost of dequantization kernels, which becomes a dominant bottleneck in sequential reasoning chains, as well as to a sequential energy amortization failure. As a result, scaling law breaking is unavoidable in practice. Our findings suggest that the industry’s “smaller-is-better” heuristic is mathematically counterproductive for complex reasoning tasks.

Keywords: Scaling law, Sustainability, Quantization, LLM

1 Introduction

The ”Scaling Law” is the foundational dogma of modern Large Language Models (LLMs) [1]. It posits that performance is a predictable function of compute and by extension, that quantization is almost a ”free lunch” for efficiency: reducing bits bb should yield a proportional reduction in energy EE and memory VV.

Consequently, the industry has widely adopted aggressive compression techniques to facilitate wider LLM deployment. For instance, the transition from 16-bit floating point (FP16) to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) or GPTQ-weighted quantization [2, 3] has become the standard protocol for serving 70B-parameter models on single consumer-grade GPUs. These methods are built on the empirical success of ’near-lossless’ quantization in general linguistic tasks, where the marginal increase in perplexity is viewed as a negligible price for the 4×\times reduction in memory footprint and the theoretical 2–4×\times gain in throughput [2, 4] . This ’linear scaling law’ paradigm assumes that efficiency gains are monotonic: as the bit-width bb decreases, the inference cost of LLM (functionally the ’cost-to-reason’ in complex tasks) should follow a downward linear trajectory.

However, we identify a fundamental breakdown of this linear scaling paradigm within multi-hop reasoning. Multi-hop reasoning [5] is the process of decomposing a complex problem into a sequential chain of intermediate logical steps, where each deduction acts as a strict prerequisite for the next. Here, the sequential accumulation of quantization noise across logical chains triggers a violation of the scaling law and we term this as Quantization Trap, where energy consumption increases and reasoning efficiency decreases for low-bit models, irrespective of model scale.

Technically, the scaling law violation (the mechanism) drives the model into this trap (the outcome), where the compressed model is strictly dominated by the original baseline.

We attribute this failure to the hardware-level ’Casting Overhead,’ where the cumulative micro-latency of de-quantizing weights back to native precision at each reasoning hop outweighs the memory bandwidth gains of compression besides rigorous analysis. Our specific contributions:

  1. 1.

    Sustainability Index (SI) framework: We develop a Sustainability Index (SI) framework to evaluate AI across the three pillars of sustainability: Economic Efficiency (ES​IE_{SI}), Social Trust (TS​IT_{SI}), and Environmental Energy (SS​IS_{SI}) to detect the Quantization Trap, in a mathematically rigorous way, which is a sub-optimal AI configurations (Sustainability Inversion).

  2. 2.

    Quantization Trap in multi-hop reasoning: We empirically identify and characterize a fundamental breaking of linear scaling laws in multi-hop reasoning. Benchmarking diverse models (e.g., Mistral-7B [6], Qwen-3 (0.6B)) on multi-hop reasoning-heavy datasets (e.g., GSM8K and MathQA) [7, 8], across NVIDIA L4, A100, H100, and Blackwell RTX 6000-pro architectures.

  3. 3.

    Theoretical foundations of the Quantization Trap: We prove a Sequential Amortization Failure theorem establishing that the Quantization Trap is structurally unavoidable in multi-hop reasoning, and demonstrate that standard mitigation strategies are mathematically incapable of restoring reasoning trust.

By exposing the breakdown of scaling laws, our findings provide a rigorous mathematical bridge between hardware telemetry and cognitive performance, enabling developers to identify and avoid Quantization Traps before committing expensive GPU resources. Ultimately, this discovery will force a fundamental shift in LLM development away from brute-force compression toward precision-aware scaling that is tailored to the actual complexity of the reasoning task, besides a mitigation path.

2 Blind spots in LLM scaling laws

The current understanding of LLM scaling is dominated by the power-law relationships established by [1] and [9], implicitly assuming that reducing numerical precision yields a guaranteed, linear reduction in hardware cost. While these scaling laws provide a recipe for pre-training, they treat ”efficiency” as a one-dimensional variable (typically FLOPs or memory footprint), effectively blinding practitioners to the non-linear latency and energy penalties incurred by hardware-level de-quantization.

Consequently, the subsequent explosion in quantization research [2, 3] has focused almost exclusively on preserving model accuracy at lower bit-widths, assuming that hardware efficiency (e.g., on GPU) improves monotonically with bit-reduction.

However, existing scaling laws and evaluation frameworks suffer from at least two critical blind spots when applied to multi-hop reasoning:

  1. 1.

    Sequential Deductive Fragility: They ignore the sequential dependencies of reasoning tasks, where quantization noise compounds at every reasoning step. This accumulation makes multi-hop reasoning uniquely fragile, as minor errors in early reasoning hops act as false premises for subsequent steps, causing irreversible logical divergence. This drives the model into the ’Quantization Trap’, which remains invisible to standard single-turn benchmarks [10].

  2. 2.

    Hardware-Software Disconnect: They ignore the ’Casting Overhead’ [11], the physical energy cost of de-quantizing low-bit weights back into native precision (FP16/BF16) during execution. This disconnect is particularly acute on widespread architectures like NVIDIA Ampere (A100) and Hopper (H100); while powerful, these architectures lack native arithmetic support for non-standard compressed formats (e.g., NF4), necessitating a mandatory, high-energy de-quantization step for every inference operation [2, 12]. As a result, the linear scaling intuition (“fewer bits ⇒\Rightarrow lower cost”) may not hold. The extra de-quantization (“casting”) work can outweigh the bandwidth savings, so using fewer bits does not reliably reduce latency or energy, and can even increase them.

To address these blind spots, we need a sustainability-focused evaluation that goes beyond single-number accuracy or perplexity. In particular, we require a unified, quantitative framework that jointly measures an LLM’s economic efficiency (throughput and deployability), trustworthiness (task performance under reasoning stress), and environmental cost (energy per query). Such a framework makes it possible to systematically detect the Quantization Trap, when apparent efficiency optimization, especially aggressive low-bit quantization-collapse under real deployment constraints and push the system into a quantization trap.

Section 3 introduces the framework of Sustainability Index (SI) to formally quantify these trade-offs.

3 The Sustainability Index (SI) Framework

The Calculus of Sustainable AI: To transcend qualitative heuristics and systematically detect structural anomalies such as the Quantization Trap, we formalize the evaluation of an AI system as a mapping ℳ:Θ→𝒱\mathcal{M}:\Theta\to\mathcal{V}. Here, Θ\Theta denotes the manifold of architectural configurations (e.g., hardware hh, precision (bit-width) pp, etc.) and 𝒱⊂[0,1]3\mathcal{V}\subset[0,1]^{3} is a bounded sustainability vector space. For any configuration θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, we define the Sustainability Vector 𝐯⁡(θ)\mathbf{v}(\theta) as:

𝐯⁡(θ)=[T⁡(θ),E⁡(θ),S⁡(θ)]⊤\mathbf{v}(\theta)=\big[T(\theta),\;E(\theta),\;S(\theta)\big]^{\top} (1)

representing the orthogonal dimensions of Trust, Efficiency, and Energy, respectively. Each dimension is normalized against a reference anchor θr​e​f\theta_{ref} (typically the full-precision baseline) to ensure scale-invariance across heterogeneous hardware.

3.1 Mathematical Axiomatization of the Pillars

I. The Trust Sustainability (TS​IT_{SI}).

In our framework, Trust is not a monolithic attribute but a context-dependent manifold defined by the functional requirements of a specific AI task topology ψ\psi. We define a set of normative metrics ℳ={m1,m2,…,mk}\mathcal{M}=\{m_{1},m_{2},\dots,m_{k}\}, where the relevant metric m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} is selected based on the risk profile of the domain. The Trust index TS​I​(θ)T_{SI}(\theta) is the preservation ratio of the primary metric relative to the anchor:

TS​I​(θ)=𝒢⁡(𝐦⁡(θ))𝒢⁡(𝐦⁡(θref))∈[0,1]T_{SI}(\theta)=\frac{\mathcal{G}\big(\mathbf{m}(\theta)\big)}{\mathcal{G}\big(\mathbf{m}(\theta_{\text{ref}})\big)}\in[0,1] (2)

where 𝐦\mathbf{m} is the vector of observed performance metrics and 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot) is a task-specific aggregation operator (e.g., accuracy, fairness-constrained utility) determined by the task topology ψ\psi.

Application to Reasoning: In logical synthesis tasks (e.g., GSM8K), we define 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot) strictly as the reasoning accuracy. This constraint reflects the domain requirement that trust is contingent on the model’s ability to maintain deductive consistency and arrive at a verifiable ground-truth solution.

Example: Evaluating Mistral-7B on an A100 GPU, the FP16 anchor achieves an accuracy of 0.43140.4314, while the 4-bit (NF4) variant yields 0.39420.3942. This results in a trust score of T⁡(θ)=0.3942/0.4314=0.914T(\theta)=0.3942/0.4314=0.914, quantifying an 8.6%8.6\% loss in deductive fidelity.

II. Economic Sustainability (ES​IE_{SI})

We quantify economic sustainability by aggregating efficiency at two distinct scales: (i) Local Algorithmic Efficiency (measured in Tokens Per Second, TPS), which rewards the model’s raw computational speed; and (ii) Global Resilience (measured in Peak VRAM, VpeakV_{\text{peak}}), which penalizes high hardware barriers to ensure deployment viability.

ES​IE_{SI} is defined as the Weighted Harmonic Mean of the normalized metrics. Let η=TPS​(θ)/TPSref\eta=\text{TPS}(\theta)/\text{TPS}_{\text{ref}} be the throughput gain and ρ=Vref/Vpeak​(θ)\rho=V_{\text{ref}}/V_{\text{peak}}(\theta) be the residency gain. The index is defined as:

ES​I​(θ)=(αη+1−αρ)−1,α∈[0,1]E_{SI}(\theta)=\left(\frac{\alpha}{\eta}+\frac{1-\alpha}{\rho}\right)^{-1},\quad\alpha\in[0,1] (3)

where α=0.5\alpha=0.5 by default. Unlike arithmetic or geometric means, the harmonic formulation is bottleneck-sensitive. It strictly penalizes deficiencies in either dimension, preventing ’extreme-case bias’ where a model might achieve high throughput simply by consuming excessive memory (or vice-versa). By explicitly including ρ\rho, our economic sustainability index penalizes the systemic ’compute divide’ [13].

III. The Energy Pillar (SS​IS_{SI}).

We define the environmental cost as the integrated power draw over the inference duration, mapped to its carbon-equivalent impact. Let P⁡(t)P(t) be the instantaneous power consumption (in Watts) tracked via hardware-level telemetry (e.g., NVML [14]). The energy-per-query ℰq\mathcal{E}_{q} is the temporal integral of power divided by the sample count NN:

ℰq​(θ)=1N​∫0𝒟P⁡(t)​𝑑t≈∑t=1𝒟Pt⋅Δ​tN\mathcal{E}_{q}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\int_{0}^{\mathcal{D}}P(t)\,dt\approx\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{D}}P_{t}\cdot\Delta t}{N} (4)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the total execution latency. To account for geographical variability in energy production, we define the Carbon-Adjusted Energy Score (CAES), denoted as χ⁡(θ)=ℰq​(θ)×γ\chi(\theta)=\mathcal{E}_{q}(\theta)\times\gamma, where γ\gamma is the grid carbon intensity (kgCO2​e/kWh\text{kgCO}_{2}\text{e}/\text{kWh} [20]).

The Energy Sustainability index SS​I​(θ)S_{SI}(\theta) is the inverse normalized ratio of CAES relative to the anchor:

SS​I​(θ)=min⁡(1,log⁡(1+χ⁡(θref))log⁡(1+χ⁡(θ))).S_{SI}(\theta)=\min\left(1,\;\frac{\log\!\bigl(1+\chi(\theta_{\text{ref}})\bigr)}{\log\!\bigl(1+\chi(\theta)\bigr)}\right). (5)

Energy-per-Query Interpretation. This formulation ensures that smaller values of SS​I​(θ)S_{SI}(\theta) denote an environmental sustainability deficit (higher emissions). Notably, if models are evaluated within the same grid infrastructure, the carbon intensity γ\gamma becomes a constant scalar that cancels out during normalization. We omit the logarithmic transform in this context because environmental impact accumulates linearly; a linear ratio preserves sensitivity to extreme energy spikes (e.g., distinguishing 10×10\times from 100×100\times deficits) that logarithmic scaling would misleadingly compress. In such cases, the index reduces to a pure energy-per-query ratio (ℰref/ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\text{ref}}/\mathcal{E}_{\theta}), allowing Joules per Query (J/QJ/Q) to serve as a direct proxy for environmental impact.

SS​IS_{SI} Example (Same grid). With the FP16 model as the anchor with energy per query: Eanchor=519.79E_{\text{anchor}}=519.79 J/query, the 4-bit (NF4) model has Emodel=1110.56E_{\text{model}}=1110.56 J/query, giving SS​I=0.468S_{SI}=0.468, suggesting worse energy emission

Energy calculation for multi-hop reasoning. We quantify SS​IS_{SI} via Hardware-Latency Integration (HLI): ℰq=(𝒫TDP⋅𝒟)/N\mathcal{E}_{q}=(\mathcal{P}_{\text{TDP}}\cdot\mathcal{D})/N, where 𝒫TDP\mathcal{P}_{\text{TDP}} is the architectural power anchor and 𝒟\mathcal{D} is high-resolution latency and NN is the sampel size in the duration. Unlike NVML, which underestimates energy by misinterpreting sequential logic-dispatch micro-stalls as ”idle savings” [15, 16], HLI treats the GPU as a committed resource throughout the reasoning duration. Because multi-hop reasoning’s high-frequency ’sawtooth’ power profile exceeds NVML’s sampling frequency [17], stochastic sensors smear transient, sub-millisecond de-quantization spikes into inter-token gaps. By integrating peak power over total latency, HLI accurately captures the energy deficit driven by casting overhead, exposing the true depth of energy use in multi-hop reasoning.

3.2 The Sustainability Manifold: Aggregation and Scaling Laws

We define the global Sustainability Index (SI) as the scalar projection of the vector 𝐯⁡(θ)\mathbf{v}(\theta) through a policy function ℱ:ℝ3→[0,1]\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to[0,1]. While traditional scaling laws focus on a 1D trajectory (e.g., bits vs. loss), our framework evaluates model configurations as points on a 3D Sustainability Manifold.

In this work, we instantiate ℱ\mathcal{F} as a Compensatory (Linear) Policy, defined as:

S​I​(θ)=𝐰⊤​𝐯​(θ),where ​∑i∈{T,E,S}wi=1SI(\theta)=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{v}(\theta),\quad\text{where }\sum_{i\in\{T,E,S\}}w_{i}=1 (6)

This formulation enables us to quantify the marginal rate of substitution between Economic efficiency, Energy, and Trust within the global sustainability score. While the weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} can be tuned to reflect specific task priorities, we adopt a balanced configuration for reasoning tasks (wT=0.34,wE=0.33,wS=0.33w_{T}=0.34,w_{E}=0.33,w_{S}=0.33) to ensure equal prioritization of all three pillars.

Remark 3.1.

While we employ a linear formulation to map the reasoning trade-off manifold, we acknowledge that safety-critical domains may necessitate a bottleneck-intolerant geometric aggregation (S​I=∏viwiSI=\prod v_{i}^{w_{i}}) to prevent efficiency gains from masking catastrophic failure.

The Scaling Monotonicity Hypothesis

The prevailing scaling paradigm relies on the Monotonicity Hypothesis: the assumption that reducing precision pp yields a monotonic increase in the scalar utility of the AI system, i.e., ∂S​I∂p<0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}<0.

In multi-hop reasoning, however, reducing pp causes the Trust (TS​IT_{SI}) and Energy (SS​IS_{SI}) indices to degrade (see the next Section). This forces their partial derivatives with respect to precision to be positive (∂TS​I∂p,∂SS​I∂p>0\frac{\partial T_{SI}}{\partial p},\frac{\partial S_{SI}}{\partial p}>0). When these penalties outweigh the marginal economic gains of compression (∂ES​I∂p<0\frac{\partial E_{SI}}{\partial p}<0), the global gradient ∇pS​I\nabla_{\!p}SI flips sign, mathematically detecting the Scaling Law Divergence inherent in a Quantization Trap.

Proposition 3.2 (Scaling Law Divergence).

Let S​I​(θ)SI(\theta) be a function of precision (bit-width) pp for a configuration θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. A Quantization Trap is identified when: ∂S​I∂p>0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}>0 signifying a fundamental breakdown of the linear scaling law. (proof in appendix)

4 Scaling Law Breaking in reasoning

In this section, we demonstrate that for multi-hopping reasoning tasks, the relationship between bit-precision and efficiency and energy is not merely sub-linear, but non-monotonic, leading to a structural ’Sustainability Inversion’: the scaling law is broken in a Quantization Trap.

4.1 Multi-Hop Reasoning and casting overhead

Multi-hop reasoning is distinguished from standard autoregressive generation by its requirement for deductive fidelity across a sequence of KK intermediate logical states, {h1,h2,…,hK}\{h_{1},h_{2},\dots,h_{K}\}. In this regime, each reasoning ”hop” hkh_{k} is a logical precursor to hk+1h_{k+1}, creating a dependency chain where the probability of reaching the correct ground-truth solution yy is the joint product of successful intermediate transitions:

P⁡(y∣x,θ)=∏k=1KP⁡(hk∣h<k,x,θ)P(y\mid x,\theta)=\prod_{k=1}^{K}P(h_{k}\mid h_{<k},x,\theta) (7)

This sequential structure makes reasoning uniquely sensitive to Scaling Law Divergence through two primary mechanisms under quantization.

Deductive Fragility. Quantization errors compound across sequential hops, where a minor shift in an early premise amplifies into ”deductive drift” and logical divergence. This may cause reasoning Trust to decrease more rapidly than in single-turn tasks, driving the positive trust gradient ∂TS​I∂p>0\frac{\partial T_{SI}}{\partial p}>0.

Temporal Accumulation. Total latency 𝒟total≈∑k=1K(τcomp+τcast)\mathcal{D}_{\text{total}}\approx\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\tau_{\text{comp}}+\tau_{\text{cast}}) aggregates native compute time τcomp\tau_{\text{comp}} and de-quantization overhead τcast\tau_{\text{cast}} across all KK sequential logical hops. Here, a hop is the atomic autoregressive forward pass (token generation). This cumulative penalty bottlenecks throughput and inflates power draw, systematically degrading both the economic (ES​IE_{SI}) and energy (SS​IS_{SI}) sustainability pillars.

Logical vs. Atomic Hops.

While the literature [18] often defines ”multi-hop reasoning” by its MM high-level logical milestones (e.g., 8–9 arithmetic operations), these milestones are physically materialized on hardware through a much longer sequence of KK atomic hops (autoregressive token generations), where K≫MK\gg M, specifically in the context of multi-hop reasoning [19]. We anchor our analysis at the atomic hop level, because it is the fundamental unit of hardware execution where the casting overhead τcast\tau_{\text{cast}} is incurred and compounded.

Casting Overhead Ratio (COR):

We formalize the hardware bottleneck via defining the Casting Overhead Ratio (C​O​RCOR)” the ratio of de-quantization latency to native compute time:

C​O​R=τcastτcompCOR=\frac{\tau_{\text{cast}}}{\tau_{\text{comp}}} (8)

The C​O​RCOR serves as a diagnostic for Casting Overhead Dominance; when C​O​R>1.0COR>1.0, the de-quantization ”tax” outweighs the actual computational work. We have following lemma and proposition related to the C​O​RCOR (proof in appendix).

Lemma 4.1 (Average Latency per hop).

Let T​P​STPS be the tokens per second. The average latency per hop is τ=1/T​P​S\tau=1/TPS.

Proposition 4.2 (C​O​RCOR Approximation).

Given a high-precision reference model (ref) and a quantized model (pp), the Casting Overhead Ratio is given by:

C​O​R≈T​P​SrefT​P​Sp−1COR\approx\frac{TPS_{\text{ref}}}{TPS_{p}}-1 (9)

4.2 Evaluation Models, Data and Hardware

To probe the limits of scaling laws, we evaluate two primary reasoning-optimized models: Mistral-7B-v0.3, a high-performance model with strong deductive capabilities, and Qwen-3-0.6B, an ultra-thin architecture designed for extreme resource-constrained deployment. We further corroborate our findings using Falcon-3B [21] to ensure that the observed Quantization Trap is a consistent phenomenon across mid-tier parameter scales.

GSM8K and MathQA [8] benchmarks: These models are tested on GSM8K (7.5K training / 1K test samples), consisting of multi-step grade-school arithmetic, and MathQA (29.8K training / 2.9K test samples), which focuses on complex algebraic transformationsc.

GSM8K consists of 8.5K high-quality, multi-step elementary school math word problems. Unlike simple question-answering, GSM8K requires models to generate a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) involving 2 to 8 arithmetic reasoning steps to arrive at a final verifiable answer. It serves as our primary probe for arithmetic noise propagation, where a single precision-induced error in an early intermediate step (e.g., a carry-over mistake) inevitably causes the entire logical chain to diverge from the ground truth.

MathQA demands significantly higher deductive depth in reasoning. MathQA stress-tests Scaling Law Divergence through complex algebraic transformations. Its extended logical chains amplify both Casting Overhead accumulation and the compounding effects of quantization noise.

Hardware Instrumentation. We mainly conduct our experiments on NVIDIA L4, A100, and H100 GPUs, spanning the Ada Lovelace, Ampere, and Hopper architectures, respectively. These platforms represent the dominant compute paths in contemporary AI deployment, ensuring that our characterization of Scaling Law Divergence reflects the physical reality of modern hardware constraints.

4.3 Sustainability Inversion: the Quantization Trap

Mistral-7B Reasoning on GSM8K.

Figure 1 summarizes the physical telemetry and sustainability analysis for Mistral-7B on GSM8K across L4, A100, and H100 GPUs. These results reveal a distinct Quantization Trap, where the linear scaling law is fundamentally broken.

Physical Proof of Scaling Law Divergence. The empirical results in Figure 1(B) provide a direct physical validation of Proposition A.1. While the traditional scaling law assumes a negative gradient (∂S​I∂p<0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}<0), where reducing precision should yield higher utility, the Final Sustainability Index (SI) exhibits a monotonic increase as precision pp is restored from 8-bit to 16-bit. Across all three architectures (L4, A100, H100), we observe S​I​(FP16)>S​I​(4-bit)>S​I​(8-bit)SI(\text{FP16})>SI(\text{4-bit})>SI(\text{8-bit}). On the H100, for instance, restoring precision from 4-bit to 16-bit yields a 31.1% improvement in global sustainability. This positive gradient, ∂S​I∂p>0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}>0, signifies that for multi-hop reasoning, the ”smaller is better” hypothesis is not only sub-optimal but mathematically inverted; increasing precision is the only path to a more efficient and sustainable system.

The Energy Paradox (SS​IS_{SI}). Under standard scaling laws, energy consumption is expected to decrease with bit-precision (J/query∝pJ/\text{query}\propto p). However, our telemetry reveals a massive Thermodynamic Spike in low-bit models. On the A100, the FP16 baseline represents the Efficiency Peak (235.47 J), while transitioning to 8-bit and 4-bit (NF4) increases energy consumption to 693.35 J and 503.06 J, respectively. This environmental deficit is most severe on the H100, where the 8-bit energy index SS​IS_{SI} drops to 0.35, representing a terminal failure in sustainability.

Decay of Deductive Trust (TS​IT_{SI}). We observe a steady decay in the Trust pillar as precision decreases, reflecting the ”deductive drift” inherent in multi-hop chains. On the A100, reasoning accuracy falls from 43.14% (FP16) to 40.86% (8-bit) and 39.42% (4-bit). While the logic remains semi-coherent, the compounding quantization noise ensures that low-bit models are less reliable for reasoning tasks.

Economic Viability Decrease (ES​IE_{SI}). Contrary to expectations, reducing precision triggers a non-monotonic throughput collapse across all architectures (Figure 1(A)). This occurs because the hardware-level Casting Overhead Ratio (COR) becomes the primary execution bottleneck; the micro-latency of de-quantizing weights outweighs the theoretical gains in memory bandwidth. Consequently, the Economic index ES​IE_{SI} for 8-bit configurations falls to ≈0.40\approx 0.40, signaling a total collapse in operational scalability for reasoning-heavy workloads.

4.3.1 The Size Paradox: Ultra-Thin Models

One might dismiss the Scaling law breaking in Quantization Trap as a byproduct of the massive memory bandwidth requirements inherent to 7B-scale models; however, by evaluating the ultra-thin Qwen-3 (0.6B), we reveal a Size Paradox: the trap is not merely a symptom of model scale, but an inescapable architectural law that becomes structurally deeper as the parameter footprint shrinks.

As illustrated in Figure  2, the 0.6B model provides the definitive evidence for Scaling Law Divergence on the GSM8K data. In Panel A, we observe a terminal Reasoning Collapse at 4-bit precision; while 8-bit maintains trust, the 4-bit variant exhibits a catastrophic drop in reasoning accuracy across all hardware.

The mechanical cause is isolated in Panel B. At the 0.6B parameter scale, τcomp\tau_{\text{comp}} becomes negligible. At the 0.6B scale, the actual matrix math is so minimal that it finishes within the GPU’s fixed latency floor for kernel dispatch [19]. So the de-quantization overhead (τcast\tau_{\text{cast}}) becomes the absolute dominant factor in the execution pipeline [11] On the A100, the Casting Overhead Ratio (C​O​RCOR) for 8-bit logic reaches an astounding 2.74, meaning the system spends nearly 3×3\times more energy emulating precision than performing deduction.

This results in the energy anomaly seen in Panel C, where the 8-bit model consumes over 17001700J per query: a 400% increase over the FP16 baseline. These results prove that for small-scale reasoners (e.g., Qwen3-0.6B), the industry-standard ”smaller-is-better” heuristic is not just sub-optimal, but physically irrational.

Scaling law breaking of Qwen-3 (0.6B) reasoning on MathQA data.To verify if higher logical complexity further compounds the hardware-level tax, we transition the ultra-thin Qwen-3 (0.6B) to the MathQA benchmark, subjecting its minimal parameter footprint to significantly deeper deductive chains.

Hardware Latency Dominance. As illustrated in Figure  3, the throughput collapse remains pervasive even at the sub-1B scale. On the A100, the 16-bit baseline achieves 611 TPS, whereas the 8-bit and 4-bit configurations are throttled to 145 and 304 TPS, respectively. This confirms that for ultra-thin reasoners, the ”actual math” executes faster than the hardware’s irreducible kernel-launch latency [19], leaving the serial de-quantization instructions as the absolute bottleneck and forcing C​O​R>1.0COR>1.0.

The Trust Divergence. On the MathQA benchmark, which demands rigorous algebraic transformations, the 4-bit variant exhibits a terminal logical divergence. While 8-bit precision maintains reasoning fidelity, the 4-bit accuracy collapses from 0.38 to 0.33 across all GPU architectures (Figure 3b). This 13% relative decay in accuracy proves that aggressive quantization is fatal for complex multi-hop tasks, where minor precision-induced errors in early premises inevitably derail long deductive paths.

Terminal Sustainability Inversion. Most critically, the Energy Paradox reaches its terminal phase on high-end architectures. On the H100 (Figure 3c), the 8-bit model consumes 1718J per query, over 4×\times the energy footprint of the 16-bit baseline (428J). Consequently, the Global Sustainability Index (S​ISI) for all low-bit configurations remains strictly below 0.80 (Figure 3f). This provides the definitive proof of the Quantization Trap: for ultra-thin models, compression is a mathematically irrational strategy that consumes more power to deliver strictly inferior logical output.

4.4 The scaling law breaking Driver: Amortization Failure

The scaling law breaking in Quantization Trap is a mechanistic consequence of Amortization Failure within the GPU’s execution pipeline. On architectures (L4/A100/H100), Tensor Cores lack a native hardware logic chain for sub-8-bit arithmetic [3, 4], necessitating the de-quantization of weights back into native precision (F​P​16FP16) before any mathematical operation can occur.

This architectural void creates a high Casting Overhead Ratio (COR). For Mistral-7B reasoning on GSM8K, the COR on H100 hardware reaches a staggering 2.45 for 8-bit precision and 1.50 for 4-bit precision. This implies that for every joule spent on actual inference, the system wastes up to 2.45 joules simply translating bits.

In high-concurrency scenarios, this overhead is ”amortized” across the batch. However, multi-hop reasoning is operationally forced into a B=1B=1 regime to satisfy sequential logic dependencies. In this state, the COR is never shared. While 4-bit (NF4) achieves a 75% bandwidth benefit, the fixed COR ensures that the cumulative casting energy Φ=∑k=1KC​O​R\Phi=\sum_{k=1}^{K}COR grows linearly with the reasoning depth KK, eventually outpacing all memory savings. We formalize this breakdown through the following theorem (proof in Appendix).

Theorem 4.3 (Sequential Amortization Failure in multi-hop reasoning).

Let ℰ⁡(p,B)\mathcal{E}(p,B) be the energy-per-query as a function of precision pp and batch size BB. For a multi-hop reasoning task on hardware with native precision π>p\pi>p, there exists a Critical Batch Threshold B∗B^{*} such that for all B<B∗B<B^{*}, the system enters a Quantization Trap defined by: ∂ℰ∂p<0.\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial p}<0.

This inversion occurs when the marginal casting overhead ϕ\phi outpaces the amortized bandwidth savings, where B∗B^{*} is uniquely determined by:

B∗=α​(π−p)ϕ⁡(h,p)B^{*}=\alpha\frac{(\pi-p)}{\phi(h,p)} (10)

Here, α\alpha is the hardware energy constant for memory movement and ϕ⁡(h,p)\phi(h,p) is the de-quantization cost for pp on architecture hh.

The Inevitability of the Quantization Trap. Theorem 4.3 mathematically guarantes the Inevitability of the Quantization Trap when batch size B<B∗B<B^{*} the Critical Batch Threshold. Under the situation, the multi-hop reasoning is structurally forced into the low-batch regime by two opposing mandates.

1. VRAM Residency (Large Models): Frontier models consume the majority of available GPU memory for weight storage. To maintain the memory-intensive cache required for long reasoning chains without triggering out-of-memory errors, the batch size must be kept at a minimum.

2. Latency Mandates (Small Models): Compact models are primarily deployed in interactive, real-time contexts. Waiting to accumulate a large batch would violate the strict latency requirements of the agent, forcing the system to process requests individually.

These constraints prevent the amortization of hardware casting overhead, ensuring that reasoning caught in Quantization Trap. Therefore, the empirical ’Sustainability Inversion’ observed is not a stochastic anomaly, but a Systemic AI Failure, a deterministic breakdown of the scaling law.

Scaling Law Divergence in multi-hop reasoning: Building on the physical constraints of the critical batch threshold B∗B^{*}, we synthesize the hardware energy deficit with the compounding requirements of logical trust to formally prove that Scaling Law Divergence is a structural necessity in multi-hop reasoning in the following theorem (proof in Appendix).

Theorem 4.4 (Scaling Law Divergence in Multi-Hop Reasoning).

For multi-hop reasoning tasks on hardware with native precision π>p\pi>p, the Scaling Law Divergence (∂S​I∂p>0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}>0) is structurally unavoidable for batch sizes B<B∗B<B^{*}.

4.5 Amortization and Quantization Trap Mitigation

Theorem 4.3 provides an increasing batch size way to decrease the casting overhead ratios. To mitigate the effects of the Quantization Trap, we investigate the scaling of batch size (BB) as a mechanism to amortize the hardware-level tax. We subject Falcon3-3B (Base and Instruct)[21] and Mistral-7B architectures to increasing batch workloads to locate the Critical Batch Threshold (B∗B^{*}) and analyze the recovery dynamics of the sustainability pillars on Blackwell RTX6000-pro.

Figure  4 illustrates the physical and reasoning response to batch scaling across three distinct architectures. The results reveal a fundamental tension between hardware throughput and logical fidelity:

Casting Dominance and Amortization. Figure  4 Column B identifies the Casting Overhead Ratio (C​O​RCOR) as the Quantization trap’s primary mechanical driver. At real-time scales (B≤16B\leq 16), all models reside in the Casting Dominance regime (C​O​R>1.0COR>1.0), where the GPU spends more energy emulating precision formats than executing logical deduction. While increasing BB amortizes this hardware tax per Theorem 4.3, Column A reveals that 8-bit configurations remain terminally slower than 16-bit baselines even at B=128B=128.

The B∗B^{*} Disparity. The threshold B∗B^{*} marks the ”sustainability equator” where quantization finally yields net gains. While Falcon3-3B reaches crossover at B∗≈64B^{*}\approx 64 (Recoverable Trap), the larger Mistral-7B remains terminally trapped (B∗>128B^{*}>128). This scale-dependent disparity proves that de-quantization overhead becomes more persistent as parameter counts grow, fundamentally breaking the scaling law for workstation-class workloads.

The Half-Mitigation Paradox. Figure  4 Column C reveals that while batching repairs throughput and energy deficits, it is functionally incapable of restoring logical fidelity. For Falcon3-3B-Instruct, the 30% logic collapse remains stagnant across all batch sizes because quantization noise ϵ\epsilon is a per-token stochastic penalty that cannot be amortized. This identifies a terminal paradox: batching may make a quantized model ”fast,” but it cannot make it ”accurate,” rendering aggressive compression a failed strategy for high-fidelity reasoning. We have the following theorem to address this.

Theorem 4.5 (Amortization-Trust Decoupling).

Let ℰ⁡(p,B)\mathcal{E}(p,B) denote the energy-per-query and T⁡(p,B)T(p,B) denote the reasoning accuracy (Trust) for a multi-hop reasoning task at precision pp and batch size BB. For any p<πp<\pi (native precision):

  1. 1.

    Efficiency Recovery: The hardware casting overhead is monotonically non-increasing with batch size, such that ∂C​O​R∂B≤0\frac{\partial COR}{\partial B}\leq 0 and limB→∞∂ℰ∂B<0\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial B}<0.

  2. 2.

    Trust Invariance: The reasoning accuracy is invariant to batch size, such that ∂T∂B=0\frac{\partial T}{\partial B}=0.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

In this work, we introduced the Sustainability Index (SI) framework and used it to demonstrate that linear scaling laws fundamentally break in the context of multi-hop reasoning. We conclude that the ”Quantization Trap” is a structural inevitability in sequential logical chains, making the industry’s ”smaller-is-better” heuristic both energy-inefficient and logically unreliable. We plan to bridge this efficiency gap by developing precision-aware mitigation strategies from a game-theoretic perspective. By viewing the allocation of numerical precision as a strategic equilibrium between hardware energy constraints and deductive trust.

Next-Generation Hardware and the Critical Batch Threshold B∗B^{*} Shift. Emerging architectures, such as NVIDIA’s Blackwell, introduce native hardware support for FP4 and FP6 precision through dedicated Tensor Core logic  [22]. This is also observed in the general <1<1 casting overhead ratios (COR) in Figure 4 column B for the quantization of 4-bits. This represents a potential mitigation path for the hardware-induced scaling law breaking. By providing native arithmetic for low-bit formats, these GPUs significantly reduce casting overhead (ϕ→0\phi\to 0), thereby pushing the Critical Batch Threshold (B∗B^{*}) toward zero. In such environments, the energy spike (SS​IS_{SI}) and throughput collapse (ES​IE_{SI}) observed in this study might be somewhat eliminated, potentially restoring the monotonic ”smaller-is-more-efficient” scaling trajectory for hardware metrics.

Nevertheless, scaling-law divergence persists at 4-bit precision due to serious reasoning accuracy collapse (e.g., Falcon3-Instruct on GSM8K, Figure 4C), which overrides the efficiency gains evidenced by its lower C​O​RCOR relative to the 8-bit variant.

Why scaling-law breaking can still persist. Importantly, hardware mitigation of casting overhead does not remove the second driver of scaling-law divergence: multi-hop deductive fragility. Quantization noise compounds across reasoning hops, degrading reasoning trust (accuracy) TS​IT_{SI} in a manner that cannot be amortized by batching (Theorem 4.5).

Moreover, multi-hop reasoning remains structurally sequential (B≈1B\approx 1) and includes fixed per-token overheads that do not scale linearly with bit-width. This can be observed in Figure 4(B), where at B=1B=1, the computation hits a fixed hardware latency floor where the non-scaling casting overhead (C​O​R>1.0COR>1.0) triggers the serious throughput collapse and 400% energy spikes observed in Figures 1 and 3.

Thus, even if future hardware reduces the severity of the Quantization Trap, the linear heuristic E∝bitsE\propto\text{bits} need not be restored; instead, precision-efficiency trade-offs remain task- and hardware-conditional on the reasoning manifold.

Appendix A Appendix

Proposition A.1 (Scaling Law Divergence).

Let S​I​(θ)SI(\theta) be a global utility function of precision pp. A Quantization Trap is identified when:

∂S​I∂p>0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}>0 (11)

signifying a fundamental breakdown of the linear scaling law.

Proof.

By definition, S​I​(p)=∑i∈{T,E,S}wi​vi​(p)SI(p)=\sum_{i\in\{T,E,S\}}w_{i}v_{i}(p) where wi>0w_{i}>0. In a standard scaling regime, utility increases as precision decreases (∂S​I∂p<0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}<0). If the constituent sustainability pillars viv_{i} (Trust, Efficiency, Energy) instead exhibit positive gradients such that their weighted sum is positive, the system enters a state of divergence. In this state, the system is strictly dominated by its high-precision counterpart, rendering bit-reduction counterproductive. ∎

Lemma A.2 (Average Latency per hop).

Let T​P​STPS be the tokens per second. The average latency per hop is τ=1/T​P​S\tau=1/TPS.

Proof.

Let KK be the total number of atomic hops (equivalent to the total tokens generated) produced during a reasoning query of total duration TT. By definition, the throughput T​P​STPS is the rate of tokens produced per second: T​P​S=KTTPS=\frac{K}{T}      The average latency per hop τ\tau is the temporal cost incurred per atomic forward pass: τ=TK.\tau=\frac{T}{K}. It follows by substitution that: τ=1K/T=1T​P​S\tau=\frac{1}{K/T}=\frac{1}{TPS}

This identity establishes that the per-hop temporal cost is the mathematical reciprocal of the system’s token production rate. ∎

Proposition A.3 (C​O​RCOR Approximation).

Given a high-precision reference model (ref) and a quantized model (pp), the Casting Overhead Ratio is given by:

C​O​R≈T​P​SrefT​P​Sp−1  COR\approx\frac{TPS_{\text{ref}}}{TPS_{p}}-1 (12)
Proof.

We decompose the average latency per hop of the quantized model, τp\tau_{p}, into its constituent hardware components: the invariant native compute time (τcomp\tau_{\text{comp}}) and the de-quantization overhead (τcast\tau_{\text{cast}}):

τp=τcomp+τcast  \tau_{p}=\tau_{\text{comp}}+\tau_{\text{cast}} (13)

For the high-precision reference model, the casting overhead is negligible (τcast≈0\tau_{\text{cast}}\approx 0), implying τref=τcomp\tau_{\text{ref}}=\tau_{\text{comp}}. Substituting this identity into the formal definition of the Casting Overhead Ratio (C​O​R=τcast/τcompCOR=\tau_{\text{cast}}/\tau_{\text{comp}}) yields:

C​O​R=τp−τrefτref=τpτref−1  COR=\frac{\tau_{p}-\tau_{\text{ref}}}{\tau_{\text{ref}}}=\frac{\tau_{p}}{\tau_{\text{ref}}}-1 (14)

Invoking the Throughput-Latency Identity (τ=1/T​P​S\tau=1/TPS), we transform the per-hop temporal costs into observable production rates:

C​O​R=1/T​P​Sp1/T​P​Sref−1  COR=\frac{1/TPS_{p}}{1/TPS_{\text{ref}}}-1 (15)

Simplifying the complex fraction, we arrive at the final approximation:

C​O​R≈T​P​SrefT​P​Sp−1  COR\approx\frac{TPS_{\text{ref}}}{TPS_{p}}-1 (16)

This identity grounds the hardware ”tax” in macro-level telemetry, proving that C​O​RCOR represents the normalized throughput deficit relative to the baseline. ∎

Theorem A.4 (Sequential Amortization Failure).

Let ℰ⁡(p,B)\mathcal{E}(p,B) be the energy-per-query as a function of precision pp and batch size BB. For a multi-hop reasoning task on hardware with native precision π>p\pi>p, there exists a Critical Batch Threshold B∗B^{*} such that for all B<B∗B<B^{*}, the system enters a a Quantization Trap defined by:

∂ℰ∂p<0  \frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial p}<0 (17)

This inversion occurs when the marginal casting overhead ϕ\phi outpaces the amortized bandwidth savings, where B∗B^{*} is uniquely determined by:

B∗=α​(π−p)ϕ⁡(h,p)  B^{*}=\alpha\frac{(\pi-p)}{\phi(h,p)} (18)

Here, α\alpha is the hardware energy constant for memory movement and ϕ⁡(h,p)\phi(h,p) is the de-quantization cost for precision pp on architecture hh.

Proof.

1. Energy Functional Decomposition:  We define total energy ℰ⁡(p,B)\mathcal{E}(p,B) for a reasoning task of depth KK. On hardware hh with native precision π\pi, energy per query is:

ℰ⁡(p,B)=K⁡[γ+α​pB+ϕ⁡(h,p)]  \mathcal{E}(p,B)=K\left[\gamma+\frac{\alpha p}{B}+\phi(h,p)\right] (19)

where γ\gamma is the static compute energy per hop, α​p/B\alpha p/B is the weight-movement energy, and ϕ\phi is the casting overhead.

The equation calculates the total energy as the product of the reasoning depth (KK) and the sum of three physical energy components required for every step in the chain.

  • •

    static compute energy per hop (γ\gamma): the constant power consumed by the GPU’s arithmetic units to execute logic gates.

  • •

    Data Movement Energy (α​pB\frac{\alpha p}{B}) per hop: The energy required to transport model weights from the memory (VRAM) to the processing cores. This is determined by the bit-count (pp), batch size (BB) and hardware energy constant for memory movement  α\alpha.

  • •

    Casting Overhead per hop (ϕ\phi): overhead from casting low-bit width to the default one.

The equation defines total query energy as the product of reasoning depth (KK) and the combined per-step costs of static hardware execution, the batch-shared energy used to move weights from memory, and the specific overhead required to translate compressed data into a format the GPU can process natively.

2. Existence of the critical batch threshold B∗B^{*}:

In the native scenario (π\pi), there is zero conversion overhead because the hardware processes the data natively (ϕ=0\phi=0). In the Low-Precision scenario (pp), the movement energy is lower, but we must add the conversion overhead (ϕ\phi).      We look for the batch size B∗B^{*} where:

EnergyLow-Bit=EnergyNative\text{Energy}_{\text{Low-Bit}}=\text{Energy}_{\text{Native}}

Mathematically, it means

K⁡[γ+α​pB∗+ϕ⁡(h,p)]=K⁡[γ+α​πB∗+0]  K\left[\gamma+\frac{\alpha p}{B^{*}}+\phi(h,p)\right]=K\left[\gamma+\frac{\alpha\pi}{B^{*}}+0\right]

Subtracting common terms γ\gamma and dividing by KK:

α​pB∗+ϕ⁡(h,p)=α​πB∗⟹ϕ⁡(h,p)=α⁡(π−p)B∗⟹B∗=α​(π−p)ϕ⁡(h,p)  \frac{\alpha p}{B^{*}}+\phi(h,p)=\frac{\alpha\pi}{B^{*}}\implies\phi(h,p)=\frac{\alpha(\pi-p)}{B^{*}}\implies B^{*}=\alpha\frac{(\pi-p)}{\phi(h,p)}

When B<B∗B<B^{*}, low-bit model will spend more energy than the original model by spending more energy.

3.  Quantization Trap Gradient:  The occurs when ∂ℰ∂p<0\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial p}<0 (see Prop.A.1.) Differentiating the energy functional:

∂ℰ∂p=K⁡[αB+∂ϕ∂p]  \frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial p}=K\left[\frac{\alpha}{B}+\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial p}\right] (20)

In sequential reasoning, the de-quantization function ϕ⁡(h,p)\phi(h,p) is a step-wise non-increasing function: larger p,  less conversion overhead: (∂ϕ/∂p≤0\partial\phi/\partial p\leq 0).

At low batch sizes (B<B∗B<B^{*}), the negative magnitude of the casting penalty |∂ϕ/∂p||\partial\phi/\partial p| exceeds the marginal bandwidth savings α/B\alpha/B, causing the gradient to sign-flip. This confirms that increasing precision pp paradoxically reduces energy. ■\blacksquare ∎

Theorem A.5 (Scaling Law Divergence in Multi-Hop Reasoning).

For multi-hop reasoning tasks on hardware with native precision π>p\pi>p, the Scaling Law Divergence (∂S​I∂p>0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}>0) is structurally unavoidable for batch sizes B<B∗B<B^{*}.

Proof.

We evaluate the three pillars of Proposition A.1 under the conditions of multi-hop reasoning:

  1. 1.

    Trust (TS​IT_{SI}): Because reasoning is a sequential product of logical transitions P⁡(y)=∏P⁡(hk)P(y)=\prod P(h_{k}), quantization noise ϵ\epsilon compounds at each hop. Thus, accuracy is a strictly non-decreasing function of precision, ∂TS​I∂p>0\frac{\partial T_{SI}}{\partial p}>0.

  2. 2.

    Energy (SS​IS_{SI}): From Theorem A.4, when B<B∗B<B^{*}, the energy-per-query ℰ\mathcal{E} decreases as precision pp increases because the hardware-level casting tax ϕ⁡(h,p)\phi(h,p) is eliminated. Since SS​IS_{SI} is inversely related to energy consumption, ∂SS​I∂p>0\frac{\partial S_{SI}}{\partial p}>0.

  3. 3.

    Economy (ES​IE_{SI}): In the sequential regime (B≈1B\approx 1), the Casting Overhead Ratio (C​O​RCOR) dominates the execution pipeline. Restoring precision removes the software-emulated de-quantization bottleneck, increasing throughput such that ∂ES​I∂p>0\frac{\partial E_{SI}}{\partial p}>0.

Since all partial derivatives are positive, the global gradient ∂S​I∂p=∑wi​∂vi∂p>0\frac{\partial SI}{\partial p}=\sum w_{i}\frac{\partial v_{i}}{\partial p}>0. By Proposition A.1, the system is trapped in a scaling law divergence. ∎

Theorem A.6 (Amortization-Trust Decoupling).

Let ℰ⁡(p,B)\mathcal{E}(p,B) denote the energy-per-query and T⁡(p,B)T(p,B) denote the reasoning accuracy for a multi-hop task at precision p<πp<\pi. For any increasing batch size BB:

  1. 1.

    Efficiency Recovery: The hardware casting overhead is monotonically non-increasing, ∂COR∂B≤0\frac{\partial\mathrm{COR}}{\partial B}\leq 0, and energy-per-query decreases, ∂ℰ∂B<0\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial B}<0.

  2. 2.

    Trust Invariance: The reasoning accuracy is invariant to batch size, ∂T∂B=0\frac{\partial T}{\partial B}=0.

Proof.

1. Proving Efficiency Recovery: In current hardware architectures, model weights are loaded and de-quantized once per batch per token. We model the per-hop latency components as:

τcomp​(p,B)=acomp​(p)⋅B,τcast​(p,B)=acast​(p)  \tau_{\mathrm{comp}}(p,B)=a_{\mathrm{comp}}(p)\cdot B,\quad\tau_{\mathrm{cast}}(p,B)=a_{\mathrm{cast}}(p) (21)

where acompa_{\mathrm{comp}} is the compute cost per example and acasta_{\mathrm{cast}} is the fixed de-quantization overhead. Substituting these into the definition of COR:

COR⁡(p,B)=acast​(p)acomp​(p)⋅B⟹∂COR∂B=−acast​(p)acomp​(p)⋅B2≤0  \mathrm{COR}(p,B)=\frac{a_{\mathrm{cast}}(p)}{a_{\mathrm{comp}}(p)\cdot B}\implies\frac{\partial\mathrm{COR}}{\partial B}=-\frac{a_{\mathrm{cast}}(p)}{a_{\mathrm{comp}}(p)\cdot B^{2}}\leq 0 (22)

This proves that the ’translation tax’ is a fixed cost shared by everyone in the batch. As you add more queries (BB), the share of the tax paid by each query shrinks, allowing hardware efficiency to recover.

Next, we define Energy-per-Query as a function of the shared casting energy (ecaste_{\mathrm{cast}}) and the compute energy (ecompe_{\mathrm{comp}}):

ℰ⁡(p,B)=K⁡(ecomp​(p)+ecast​(p)B)⟹∂ℰ∂B=−K⋅ecast​(p)B2<0  \mathcal{E}(p,B)=K\left(e_{\mathrm{comp}}(p)+\frac{e_{\mathrm{cast}}(p)}{B}\right)\implies\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial B}=-\frac{K\cdot e_{\mathrm{cast}}(p)}{B^{2}}<0 (23)

Because the total energy to move and de-quantize weights is constant, processing more queries simultaneously reduces the energy ’bill’ for each individual query.

2. Proving Trust Invariance: Reasoning accuracy T⁡(p,B)T(p,B) is determined by the model’s logits, which are a function of the precision pp. For a fixed decoding algorithm, the output y^\hat{y} for an input xx is:

y^=f⁡(x,p)  \hat{y}=f(x,p) (24)

Since f⁡(x,p)f(x,p) has no dependency on the batch size BB (Assumption of Semantic Independence), the prediction for any query in the batch remains identical regardless of parallelization:

T⁡(p,B)=1N​∑i=1N𝕀⁡(y^p,i=yi∗)⟹∂T∂B=0  T(p,B)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_{p,i}=y^{*}_{i})\implies\frac{\partial T}{\partial B}=0 (25)

This proves the decoupling. Batching makes the hardware faster, but it does not make the model smarter. The reasoning errors caused by 4-bit quantization are a permanent property of the bits (pp), not the batch (BB). Mitigation via batching fixes the energy ’Trap’ but leaves the ’Deductive Fragility’ untouched. ∎
